//: TRIGGERS — your project's own actions, attached to moments in the loop.
Copy to .game_loop/triggers.json (gitignored) and edit. Scripts live in
.game_loop/triggers.d/ (also gitignored). Both are SITE wiring: they name paths, rooms and
sometimes credentials that belong to one machine, not to the product.
WHY THIS EXISTS. Some things worth doing at a moment in the loop cannot ship as a rule, because
they depend on infrastructure most installs do not have — a chat room, a ticket tracker, a
metrics endpoint. game_loop owns the MOMENT; you own what happens there.
THE CONTRACT
* the event payload arrives as JSON on stdin (the same shape Claude Code hands its hooks)
* stdout comes back to the agent and is printed — this is how a trigger TELLS you things
* env: GAME_LOOP_EVENT, GAME_LOOP_ROOT (the .game_loop dir), GAME_LOOP_REPO (the repo root),
GAME_LOOP_SESSION and GAME_LOOP_SESSION_DIR — WHICH SESSION this is speaking for. One
checkout can hold many concurrent sessions doing unrelated work, so anything you read or
write per-run must be scoped by these rather than globbed across the repo. EMPTY means
UNKNOWN (the legacy repo-global paths), never a session whose name is the empty string:
decline rather than guess. The waiting probe gets the same two, plus GAME_LOOP_TRANSCRIPT.
* a non-zero exit is reported loudly and NEVER blocks the verb — the work outranks the
announcement, and a broadcast that can veto what it reports on is a guard blocking its own fix
* timeout_sec defaults to 20
MOMENTS AVAILABLE
harden   — a learning was just encoded. Payload: learning, general, artifact, mechanism, rung,
project, session. `--general` is the transferable form, and is null when not given.
stepback — a retro just began, BEFORE its output. Payload: notes, project, session,
trans_since, work_since. The moment to pull in what others have learned.
confidence — a commit was just marked beta or stable. Payload: level, sha, tag, ref, notes,
project, session. This is the instant 'ready for consumers' stops being an
intention and becomes a fact about a sha, so anything that DISTRIBUTES this
project belongs here: a package manager, a mirror, an announcement. It is also
the last honest moment to ask whether consumers can FIND what they are given —
see the documentation example below. Order matters within an event: they run top
to bottom, so put the checks above the publish.
session_start — a session just started, or was compacted. Payload: source (startup / resume /
clear / compact), project, session. THE ONE MOMENT THAT IS NOT A VERB SOMEBODY
TYPED, and the only one where the session ACTS on its own behalf instead of being
told things: registering with a local tool, joining a room, claiming a name. Its
stdout is APPENDED to the status block the harness already injects, so an
attachment can both act and report what it did in one text.
Three things to know before you attach here, because this moment is on the path
every session crosses:
* it fires at EVERY start and EVERY compaction — make the command idempotent, or
branch on `source`. 'Once per project' is yours to enforce, not the harness's.
* the timeout budget is PER attachment and nothing caps the sum, so N slow
attachments cost N timeouts before the session sees a word. Keep them short.
* `"session_start": false` in config.json switches the whole moment off. Then
nothing attached here can ever fire — `status` says SWITCHED OFF rather than
letting it read as an attachment that is merely patient.
`game_loop status` lists what you have attached and names anything that has never fired.
Configured and working are different claims, and only one of them is visible by default.

harden.name: example-append-to-a-file
harden.command: python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); g=d.get('general'); print('nothing to share' if not g else open('/tmp/learnings.md','a').write(g+chr(10)) and 'shared')"

//: ACT ONCE, THEN SAY YOU DID. The marker file is the whole example: this moment fires on
every start and every compaction, so an attachment that is not idempotent does its
one-time act several times a day. Writing the marker under $GAME_LOOP_ROOT keeps it with
the checkout it is true of; put it under $GAME_LOOP_SESSION_DIR instead if the act is
once per SESSION rather than once per project.
It prints, and that is not decoration: an act nobody can see happened is the failure this
harness exists to prevent. The line lands in the same context the session reads first.
session_start.name: example-act-once-per-project
session_start.command: m="$GAME_LOOP_ROOT/probe/session-start-acted"; [ -f "$m" ] && exit 0; date > "$m"; echo "acted once for this project (delete $m to do it again)"

stepback.name: example-read-something
stepback.command: echo 'whatever this prints is shown to the agent before it reflects'

//: DOES THE DOCUMENTATION KNOW ABOUT THIS RELEASE? Worth stealing, because the failure it
catches is quiet and universal: a feature lands, its design gets written up somewhere
deep, and the two files a human and an agent actually START from never hear about it.
This repo shipped four user-facing features that way in a single week.
The check is the ungameable half — every option and config key the CODE defines, against
your documentation files. Prose cannot satisfy it: the name appears or it does not. What
it cannot check is the larger half, and say so where you use it: whether the docs are
correct, whether they EXPLAIN the thing or merely name it, or whether they still describe
what the code does. A mention is the floor, not the goal.
Two tiers is what makes it useful — 'written down somewhere' and 'reachable' are
different properties, and only the second is worth anything to a consumer.
confidence.name: example-undocumented-surface
confidence.command: grep -ho 'add_argument("--[a-z-]*"' src/*.py | sed 's/.*"\(--[a-z-]*\)"/\1/' | sort -u | while read -r o; do grep -qF -- "$o" README.md || echo "UNDOCUMENTED: $o"; done; echo '(checks that a name APPEARS, never that the prose is right)'
